title: What might have been
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: law + kuntu qad + V-past + , + la- + V-past

rules.text: kāna qad + a past verb is the PLUPERFECT — one step behind the past: kāna qad dhahaba, he had gone. L3-M7 opened qad in front of a past to mean already; kāna is what pushes the whole thing further back.

The person lives in kāna and again in the far verb, never in the frame between them. kuntu qad akaltu marks I twice and both ends must agree; kāna yajibu marks nobody at all and is frozen in the he-form.
kāna + sa- + a present verb is the was-going-to: kuntu sa-attaṣil. L1-M6's future put behind a past kāna — the plan existed, and the plan did not happen. Nothing about the verb under sa- changes.
kāna ʿalayya an is the personal past obligation: L1-M7's ʿalā with a pronoun on it — ʿalayya on me, ʿalayka on you, ʿalayhi on him. Unlike kāna yajibu, this frame does carry the person.

English would have, should have and could have are three different auxiliaries. Arabic has none of them: every one is kāna in front of something this ladder already owns — a past verb, a sa- future, or an obligation frame.

One kāna is the whole auxiliary. Because it is doing so much work here, learners stack it — kuntu kāna, kāna sa-kāna — and neither is a sentence. If kāna is already there, the second one is the mistake.
After an the verb is present-SHAPED whatever the English tense says, and after qad it is past. The tense of the English sentence decides nothing at all about the shape of the second verb.
L3-M4's conditional does not change here. law still opens the condition and the answer clause still wears la- on a plain past verb, however long the condition in front of it has become.
The past obligation is negated on kāna, not on the frame: lam yakun yajibu an taqūl dhālika. L3-M4's lam turns kāna into yakun, and yajibu behind it is untouched.

sentences.cue: He had gone before the meeting

words.note: L3-M7's qad, one step further back: kāna in front of it puts a finished event behind another finished event. kānat qad for a woman.

sentences.trap: English needs two words for this — had gone. Arabic needs kāna in front of the past it already writes, and dhahaba itself does not change shape at all.
sentences.sound: KĀ-na qad DHA-ha-ba: three short words, and qad is said quickly enough to sound joined to the verb behind it.

variations.cue: She had gone before the meeting
variations.changed: the person: he → she, in kāna and in the far verb both

variations.cue: He had eaten before the party
variations.changed: the event and the landmark: going before a meeting → eating before a party

mistake.why: Without qad this is not the pluperfect — kāna and a bare past verb read as two loose events rather than one that finished before the other. qad is what stacks them.

sentences.usage: Putting one past event behind another: what was already done by the time something else happened.
sentences.mnemonic: kāna carries the person, qad carries the already.

sentences.cue: I had already eaten before the party

words.note: The person is written twice — in kuntu and again in akaltu — and both ends have to agree. qad in the middle never changes.

sentences.trap: English marks the person once, in I. Arabic marks it in kuntu and again in the far verb, and a mismatch — kuntu qad akala — is a different sentence, not a slip.
sentences.sound: KUN-tu qad a-KAL-tu — the two -tu endings are the person, said at both ends of the frame.

variations.cue: You had already eaten before the party
variations.changed: the person: I → you, in both verbs at once

variations.cue: I had studied before the exam
variations.changed: what and when: eating before a party → studying before the exam

mistake.why: kuntu says I and akala says he. The frame does not carry the person for the verb behind it, so both ends have to say the same thing.

sentences.usage: Saying you had already done a thing, so an offer or a plan is no longer needed.
sentences.mnemonic: Person at both ends, qad in the middle.

sentences.display: law kuntu qad dhahabtu mubakkiran, la-raʾaytu al-mudīr
sentences.script: لو كنت قد ذهبت مبكراً، لرأيت المدير
sentences.cue: If I had gone early, I would have seen the manager
sentences.literal: If I-was already I-went early, then-I-saw the-manager

words.note: L3-M4's la- is still the answer marker and it still sits on a plain past verb. Nothing about law changes because the condition in front of it got longer.

sentences.trap: English stacks would have on top of a past. Arabic's answer clause is exactly what L3-M4 already taught — la- on an ordinary past verb — however long the condition has become.
sentences.sound: la-ra-AY-tu: the la- is one light syllable glued to the verb, never a word standing on its own.

variations.display: law kuntu qad dhahabtu mubakkiran, la-akaltu maʿaka
variations.script: لو كنت قد ذهبت مبكراً، لأكلت معكَ
variations.cue: If I had gone early, I would have eaten with you
variations.changed: the answer clause: seeing the manager → eating with you

variations.display: law kuntu qad waṣaltu mubakkiran, la-raʾaytu al-mudīr
variations.script: لو كنت قد وصلت مبكراً، لرأيت المدير
variations.cue: If I had arrived early, I would have seen the manager
variations.changed: the condition: going early → arriving early

mistake.display: law kuntu qad dhahabtu mubakkiran, raʾaytu al-mudīr
mistake.script: لو كنت قد ذهبت مبكراً، رأيت المدير
mistake.why: Dropping la- leaves two plain past clauses side by side, which reads as a report of what happened. la- is what marks the half that did not.

sentences.usage: Regretting a decision out loud: naming the thing you did not do, and what it cost you.
sentences.mnemonic: Longer condition, same short answer: la- and a past verb.

sentences.display: kāna yajibu an adhhab ilā al-mustashfā
sentences.script: كان يجب أن أذهب إلى المستشفى
sentences.cue: I should have gone to the hospital
sentences.literal: Was it-is-necessary that I-go to the-hospital

words.note: L3-M2's yajibu with kāna in front of it, frozen in the he-form whoever is speaking. The person appears only in the far verb: adhhab.

sentences.trap: English says I should have and puts the person on the modal. Arabic puts nothing on the frame — kāna yajibu never changes — and only adhhab says who.
sentences.sound: KĀ-na YA-ji-bu an AD-hab — four beats, with the an said so lightly it almost joins the verb.

variations.display: kāna yajibu an tadhhab ilā al-mustashfā
variations.script: كان يجب أن تذهب إلى المستشفى
variations.cue: You should have gone to the hospital
variations.changed: who should have gone: I → you, in the far verb only

variations.cue: I should have studied more
variations.changed: the obligation itself: going to the hospital → studying more

mistake.display: kuntu yajibu an adhhab ilā al-mustashfā
mistake.script: كنت يجب أن أذهب إلى المستشفى
mistake.why: The frame does not take a person. kuntu yajibu puts I on a verb already frozen in the he-form; the frame is kāna yajibu for everybody.

sentences.usage: Saying, after the fact, that you should have done something — the ordinary spoken regret.
sentences.mnemonic: The frame is frozen; the person waits at the far verb.

sentences.cue: I had to pay the bill

words.note: Here the person IS in the frame: L1-M7's ʿalā with a pronoun on it — ʿalayya me, ʿalayka you, ʿalayhi him — and the far verb repeats it.

sentences.trap: English had to and should have are two modals of the same family. Arabic splits them differently: kāna yajibu is the impersonal one, kāna ʿalayya names whose duty it was.
sentences.sound: KĀ-na ʿa-LAY-ya — the ʿayn is the throat sound, and the -yya at the end is held: ʿalayya, not ʿalaya.

variations.cue: You had to pay the bill
variations.changed: whose duty: mine → yours, in the frame and in the verb

variations.cue: He had to pay the rent
variations.changed: whose duty and what for: mine and the bill → his and the rent

mistake.why: After an the verb is present-shaped whatever the English tense says. dafaʿtu is a finished past and cannot stand behind an.

sentences.usage: Explaining an obligation that is over — often the reason you could not do something else.
sentences.mnemonic: The duty sits ON you: ʿalayya, ʿalayka, ʿalayhi.

sentences.display: lam yakun yajibu an taqūl dhālika
sentences.script: لم يكن يجب أن تقول ذلك
sentences.literal: Not it-was it-is-necessary that you-say that

words.note: Negating the frame, not the verb: L3-M4's lam turns kāna into yakun and the whole obligation goes away. yajibu behind it is untouched.

sentences.trap: English negates the modal itself — shouldn't have. Arabic negates kāna, which is why the negative lands three words away from the thing that did not have to happen.
sentences.sound: lam YA-kun YA-ji-bu: three words with no pause, and the -n of yakun running straight into the y- of yajibu.

variations.cue: I shouldn't have gone
variations.changed: who: you → I, in the far verb

variations.display: lam yakun yajibu an tadfaʿ al-fātūra
variations.script: لم يكن يجب أن تدفع الفاتورة
variations.cue: You didn't have to pay the bill
variations.changed: the obligation: saying that → paying the bill

mistake.why: lam attaches to kāna here, not to yajibu. Negating the frame directly leaves the sentence with no past in it and no obligation to cancel.

sentences.usage: Telling somebody, gently or otherwise, that a thing was said or done when it need not have been.
sentences.mnemonic: Negate the kāna, leave the yajibu alone.

sentences.cue: I was going to call you, but I forgot

words.note: L1-M6's sa- future put behind kāna: the plan is in the past and it did not happen. The verb under sa- keeps its ordinary present shape.

sentences.trap: English needs two auxiliaries — was going to. Arabic needs kāna plus the sa- it already has, and the verb itself does not move at all.
sentences.sound: KUN-tu sa-at-ta-ṢIL: the sa- is one quick syllable, and what follows it is the plain present.

variations.cue: You were going to call, but you forgot
variations.changed: the person: I → you, in kāna and under sa- both

variations.cue: He was going to call you, but he forgot
variations.changed: the person: I → he, all the way through the sentence

mistake.why: One kāna is the whole auxiliary. Stacking a second — kuntu kāna, kāna sa-kāna — is the commonest over-reach in this module, and it is not a sentence.

sentences.usage: Excusing a plan that fell through, without saying whose fault it was.
sentences.mnemonic: Past kāna, future sa-, one event that never happened.

sentences.cue: I regretted it because I didn't go with you

words.note: An ordinary past verb, not a frame: nadimtu I, nadima he, nadimat she. What is regretted hangs off L1-M9's li-ʾanna behind it.

sentences.trap: English regret takes an object — I regret it. Arabic hangs the reason off li-ʾanna instead, and L4-M2's rule still holds: that reason clause cannot be moved to the front.
sentences.sound: na-DIM-tu: short a, short i, and the -tu that means I, exactly as in dhahabtu.

variations.cue: He regretted it because he didn't go with me
variations.changed: the person, in the verb and in the reason clause both

variations.cue: I regretted it because I didn't study
variations.changed: the reason: not going with you → not studying

mistake.why: lam takes the present-shaped verb, never the past one — L3-M4's rule, unchanged. lam dhahabtu is two pasts fighting over one slot.

sentences.usage: Owning a small failure to somebody's face, which is what this level's register is for.
sentences.mnemonic: nadimtu, then the reason — never the reason first.

sentences.cue: I missed the train, and I missed the chance

words.cue: it escaped me / I missed it
words.note: Arabic puts the thing that got away in the subject slot: literally the train escaped me. fātatnī is the feminine, for a feminine noun like al-furṣa.
Feminine, which is why the verb in front of it is fātatnī and not fātanī. The plural is furaṣ.

sentences.trap: English makes you the subject — I missed the train. Arabic reverses it: the train is the subject and you are the object stuck on the end of the verb as -nī.
sentences.sound: FĀ-ta-nī: long ā, then the -nī that means me. fātatnī adds the feminine -at- in the middle.

variations.cue: I missed the train and I missed the meeting
variations.changed: the second thing missed: a feminine noun → a masculine one, so the verb loses its -at-

variations.cue: I missed a lovely opportunity
variations.changed: the-opportunity → an opportunity, with an adjective behind it

mistake.why: The English shape — I as the subject — does not carry over. anā is already inside the -nī on the verb, and putting it in front makes two subjects for one train.

sentences.usage: Reporting a loss that was nobody's fault, or presenting it that way.

sentences.display: kāna al-qarār khaṭaʾ, wa kāna yajibu an aqūl lā
sentences.script: كان القرار خطأ، وكان يجب أن أقول لا
sentences.cue: The decision was a mistake, and I should have said no
sentences.literal: Was the-decision mistake, and was it-is-necessary that I-say no

words.note: Masculine, so the kāna in front of it stays kāna. The plural qarārāt is what a meeting produces.

sentences.trap: English would fold the whole regret onto one modal — I shouldn't have decided that. Arabic states the verdict first and hangs the obligation frame behind it, with kāna doing both jobs.
sentences.sound: al-qa-RĀR: the stress is on the long ā at the end. khaṭaʾ finishes on a hamza — a catch in the throat, not a vowel.

variations.display: kāna al-qarār ṣaḥīḥ, wa kuntu qad qultu naʿam
variations.script: كان القرار صحيح، وكنت قد قلت نعم
variations.cue: The decision was right, and I had said yes
variations.changed: the verdict and the frame: a mistake and should-have → right and had-already

variations.display: kāna al-qarār khaṭaʾ, wa kāna ʿalayya an aqūl lā
variations.script: كان القرار خطأ، وكان عليّ أن أقول لا
variations.cue: The decision was a mistake, and it was on me to say no
variations.changed: the obligation frame: the impersonal one → the one that names whose duty it was

mistake.display: kāna al-qarār khaṭaʾ, wa yajibu an aqūl lā
mistake.script: كان القرار خطأ، ويجب أن أقول لا
mistake.why: Without the second kāna the sentence turns into a present obligation — I have to say no — and the regret disappears. kāna is the whole difference.

sentences.usage: Closing an account of something that went wrong: the verdict, then what you should have done.
sentences.mnemonic: One kāna for the verdict, one for the regret.
